textbook:
Clean cutaway textbook illustration of ONE human Type IIa skeletal muscle fibre (fast oxidative-glycolytic fibre), centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous negative space around the structures so labels can be attached later. The illustration's own neutral dark charcoal background must extend and touch all four edges of the canvas, filling it completely corner to corner. Do NOT draw any border line, rectangle outline, frame, mat, margin band, vignette or letterbox bar around the artwork, and do NOT draw the picture as a sheet or card lying on a surface.

HOUSE LOOK — match a refined educational plate exactly: a MUTED, slightly desaturated palette of soft dusty tints (never bright primary or cartoon colours), THIN clean outlines (never heavy black cartoon strokes), gentle soft shading with subtle dimensionality, and each structure its own distinct soft colour fill.

FRAMING (critical, this failed on the last two attempts — fix it this time): the fibre must be drawn SO LARGE AND SO ZOOMED IN that it is physically impossible to fit an end-cap inside the canvas. Do NOT draw a rounded end-cap or oval disc AT ALL, anywhere, under any circumstances — not even partially. The tube's two long straight edges must run from one corner of the canvas to the opposite corner, filling the diagonal, with the tube's own body touching or crossing all four sides of the square canvas near the corners. Picture a fat diagonal stripe of tube-body filling most of the frame, so wide and so close to the viewer that both of its ends are pushed completely outside the visible picture — you should not be able to see where the tube starts or stops, only its long straight sides and the banded surface between them. If you can see background beyond either tip of the tube, the tube is drawn too small — make it at least 40% larger and re-crop tighter around its middle section.

BAND DENSITY: draw at least TWENTY narrow cross-bands along the visible length, closely spaced like fine engraving lines — not four or five wide paint stripes. The bands should look numerous and fine, repeating rapidly along the tube, the way real sarcomere striation looks under magnification: a dense fine ladder, not a few thick painted rings.

CROSS-STRIATION (the single most important instruction — read carefully): the fibre's surface and interior are marked by narrow bands that wrap around the tube and cross its ENTIRE width at each point along its length, like the printed rings on a drinking straw, the rungs of a ladder laid along the tube, or the fret markings on a drum — each band is SHORT (only as wide as the tube) and repeats close together, one after another, all the way along the visible length, so that at any point you are looking at, a complete band spans from one long edge of the tube to the other, perpendicular to the direction the tube runs. Colour the bands in an alternating pattern: a slightly deeper dusty-rose A band next to a paler pink I band, with a fine slate-blue Z-line at the centre of every I band — dozens of these paired bands, evenly spaced, covering the whole visible length with no gaps or smooth patches. Underneath this banding, faint parallel guide-lines running lengthwise along the tube (the myofibrils) may be visible, but the banding itself is what reads first and must never be reduced to a few lengthwise colour stripes running along the tube's direction — it is cross-bands, not a lengthwise grain.

COLOUR: the fibre's overall tone is a warm PALE ROSE-PINK — visibly pinker and deeper than a pale cream fibre, but clearly lighter than a deep-red fibre — because this is the middle fibre type, part-oxidative and part-glycolytic. It is a MID-SIZED fibre, narrower than the widest fibre type and wider than the narrowest.

SURFACE AND INTERIOR:
- A thin teal-blue SARCOLEMMA outlines the whole cylinder.
- Along the fibre's outer rim, spaced out one after another, draw AT LEAST SEVEN separate oval, flattened, blue-violet NUCLEI, every single one tucked immediately under the sarcolemma at the periphery, oriented lengthwise with the fibre. Do NOT draw a single nucleus in the middle of the cell.
- The cross-banding described above covers the ENTIRE outer surface of the tube along its whole visible length, not only a windowed strip. In a neat long cutaway window along part of the fibre (in addition to the surface banding), reveal parallel MYOFIBRILS carrying the same cross-banding, with amber-ochre MITOCHONDRIA gathered in loose, moderate clusters between them — visibly more numerous than a few scattered singles, but not forming a dense solid carpet — a comfortable middle ground between sparse and packed. Dust a modest scatter of small golden-tan GLYCOGEN GRANULE dots between the myofibrils, present but not overwhelming.
- Alongside the fibre, outside the sarcolemma, run one CAPILLARY (a smooth tube with a fine crimson lumen) tracking the fibre's length — draw it a touch more substantial than a bare thread, reflecting a moderate blood supply, but still clearly a single slender vessel, not a network.

DO NOT draw: a rounded end cap or closed disc at either end; any branching, forking, or Y-shape; intercalated discs; a single central nucleus or any nucleus not touching the rim; deep red colouration or pale cream/near-white colouration (this fibre is rose-pink, between the two); a dense wall-to-wall carpet of mitochondria or only one or two isolated mitochondria; a smooth unstriated patch anywhere along the fibre; a cell wall, nucleoid, plasmids, flagella or cilia. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, scale bars or watermarks anywhere in the image. The CAPILLARY must be a smooth, continuously curving vessel of a single uniform crimson tone throughout its length — never a candy-cane, barber-pole, segmented rod, swab stick, thermometer, or anything with alternating stripes or beads.
sem:
Photorealistic false-colour SCANNING ELECTRON MICROGRAPH of ONE human Type IIa skeletal muscle fibre (fast oxidative-glycolytic fibre), centered in a square 1:1 1080x1080 frame with generous empty margin. Fill the whole square edge to edge with NO border, frame, vignette or letterbox bar, and do not render the image as a plate lying on a surface.

FRAMING (critical, this failed badly on a sibling render — fix it from the start): the fibre must be drawn SO LARGE AND SO ZOOMED IN that it is physically impossible to fit an end-cap inside the canvas. Do NOT draw a rounded end-cap or closed disc AT ALL, anywhere, under any circumstances — not even partially. The tube's two long straight edges must run from one corner of the canvas to the opposite corner, filling the diagonal, with the tube's own body touching or crossing all four sides of the square canvas near the corners. Picture a fat diagonal band of tube-body filling most of the frame, so wide and so close to the viewer that both of its ends are pushed completely outside the visible picture — you should not be able to see where the tube starts or stops, only its long straight sides and the banded surface between them. If you can see background beyond either tip of the tube, the tube is drawn too small — make it at least 40% larger and re-crop tighter around its middle section. The specimen rests on a subtly textured flat substrate; it never forks or tapers into a Y, and it is a MID-SIZED fibre — narrower than the widest fibre type, wider than the narrowest — with a smooth-surfaced, distinctly PALE ROSE-PINK false-colour tone (visibly pinker/deeper than a pale cream fibre, clearly lighter than a deep-red fibre).

BAND DENSITY: draw at least TWENTY narrow cross-bands along the visible length, closely spaced like fine engraving lines or ridges — not four or five wide stripes. The bands should look numerous and fine, repeating rapidly along the tube, the way real sarcomere striation looks under magnification: a dense fine ladder/comb pattern, not a few thick painted rings.

SURFACE TEXTURE (the single most important instruction): render true 3D surface relief as a dense series of fine transverse RIDGES that each wrap all the way around the fibre's width, crossing it from one long edge to the other, evenly spaced and repeating one after another along the ENTIRE visible length — like the printed rings on a drinking straw or the treads of a corrugated pipe seen end-on-to-side. This ribbing must read as short cross-bands stacked along the tube, never as a few long ridges running parallel to the tube's own direction, and it must never stop or smooth out partway along the fibre.

Along the fibre's flanks, spaced out one after another, show several long, shallow, oval BULGES in the surface, each one sitting exactly at the rim where an underlying peripheral nucleus pushes up against the sarcolemma from just inside — at least six or seven of them, spread along the length, never a single bulge in the middle. A capillary vessel of moderate thickness (reflecting a middling blood supply, thicker than a bare thread but still a single slender vessel) may lie alongside part of the fibre, partially in focus. Crisp fine surface texture, shallow depth of field so the far ends fall softly out of focus, cool studio microscopy lighting with a gentle rim light.

False-colour palette: warm pale rose-pink fibre surface, a slightly cooler rose in the ridge grooves, on a neutral pale grey substrate and a dark uncluttered charcoal background.

DO NOT render: any branching or Y-fork; a rounded tip or end-face at either end; a smooth unribbed patch anywhere along the fibre; deep red or pale cream/near-white surface tones; a few long ridges running the length of the tube instead of many short cross-bands; duplicated specimens; any floating debris. Single specimen only, clearly dominant in the frame. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, labels, arrows, scale bars, instrument data bars or watermarks anywhere in the image.
watercolor:
Hand-painted WATERCOLOUR naturalist scientific plate of ONE human Type IIa skeletal muscle fibre (fast oxidative-glycolytic fibre), in the composition of a 19th-century scientific atlas but anatomically modern and correct. Square 1:1, 1080x1080.

PAPER RULE (most important): the warm, softly mottled AGED PAPER is the background and it must FILL THE ENTIRE FRAME, edge to edge and corner to corner, with its grain and foxing running right off all four sides. Do NOT paint the artwork as a separate sheet, card or page lying on a table, desk or any surface. NO mat, NO border, NO frame, NO drop shadow, NO torn or deckled paper edge, NO grey or dark panel around a sheet, NO vignette, NO letterbox bars.

FRAMING (critical, this failed badly on a sibling render — fix it from the start): the fibre must be drawn SO LARGE AND SO ZOOMED IN that it is physically impossible to fit an end-cap inside the canvas. Do NOT draw a rounded end-cap or closed disc AT ALL, anywhere, under any circumstances — not even partially. The tube's two long straight edges must run from one corner of the canvas to the opposite corner, filling the diagonal, with the tube's own body touching or crossing all four sides of the square canvas near the corners. Picture a fat diagonal band of tube-body filling most of the frame, so wide and so close to the viewer that both of its ends are pushed completely outside the visible picture — you should not be able to see where the tube starts or stops, only its long straight sides and the banded surface between them. If you can see background beyond either tip of the tube, the tube is drawn too small — make it at least 40% larger and re-crop tighter around its middle section. It is painted in rich translucent washes with fine ink linework for the outlines. The fibre keeps a perfectly UNIFORM diameter along its whole visible length — it must not narrow, pinch, neck down, taper, or hourglass anywhere in the middle; it stays a plain straight-sided cylinder from one visible end to the other, with the cutaway simply a rectangular window cut lengthwise into the side of that straight tube. It reads as a MID-SIZED fibre — narrower than the widest of the three human fibre types, wider than the narrowest — painted a warm PALE ROSE-PINK wash throughout, visibly pinker/deeper than a pale-cream wash and clearly lighter than a deep-red wash, with a soft darker wash halo laid directly on the paper behind it.

BAND DENSITY: draw at least TWENTY narrow cross-bands along the visible length, closely spaced like fine engraving lines or ridges — not four or five wide stripes. The bands should look numerous and fine, repeating rapidly along the tube, the way real sarcomere striation looks under magnification: a dense fine ladder/comb pattern, not a few thick painted rings.

CROSS-STRIATION (the single most important instruction): paint narrow bands that wrap around the tube and cross its ENTIRE width at every point along its length — like the printed rings on a drinking straw, the rungs of a ladder laid along the tube, or fine comb-teeth pressed across it. Each band is SHORT (spanning only the tube's width) and repeats closely, one after another, the whole visible length: a slightly deeper dusty-rose A band, a pale pink I band, a fine ink Z-line down the centre of each I band, all in register, with no gaps. Faint fine ink lines running lengthwise beneath the banding may suggest the myofibrils, but the banding itself must read first, as cross-bands — never reduce it to a few lengthwise painted stripes running along the tube's own direction. This cross-banding covers the ENTIRE visible length of the tube, not only a small window.

Interior: along the fibre's outer edge, spaced out one after another, AT LEAST SEVEN separate small oval violet-washed NUCLEI, every one sitting right at the rim under the painted sarcolemma line — never a single nucleus painted in the middle; ochre MITOCHONDRIA dots gathered in loose, moderate clusters between the myofibrils — more numerous than a few scattered singles, but never a dense solid mass; a modest scatter of small golden-tan GLYCOGEN GRANULE dots stippled between the myofibrils; and, running alongside the fibre, one painted CAPILLARY line with a fine crimson core, a touch more substantial than a bare thread.

Muted botanical-plate palette: pale rose-pink, dusty rose, cream, ochre, golden-tan, soft slate blue and violet, on warm cream paper.

DO NOT paint: a rounded cap or closed disc at either end; any branching or Y-fork; intercalated discs; a single central nucleus or any nucleus not at the rim; deep red or pale cream/near-white washes; a dense solid mass of mitochondria or only one or two isolated ones; a smooth unstriated patch anywhere along the fibre; a cell wall, nucleoid, plasmids, flagella or cilia; any hourglass/necking of the tube. Absolutely NO text, letters, numbers, handwriting, labels, arrows, scale bars, signatures or watermarks anywhere in the image. The CAPILLARY must be a smooth, continuously curving vessel of a single uniform crimson tone throughout its length — never a candy-cane, barber-pole, segmented rod, swab stick, thermometer, or anything with alternating stripes or beads.
